title: Recognition of multimolecular G-quadruplex regulates phase separation of cockayne syndrome B.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Opened the Zenodo record (27 files, 82.6 MB total, CC-BY-4.0) and downloaded and parsed 6 of them: four Excel workbooks, one CSV and one tab-delimited text file. Read sheet names, header rows and first rows: they are per-droplet ImageJ (image analysis software) measurement blocks (Area, Mean intensity, Circularity, Aspect Ratio, Solidity, Radius, Volume uM^3) and raw FRAP (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching) traces, laid out as repeated 'REP 1 / REP 2' blocks spanning up to 66 columns per sheet. Counted rows per sheet (e.g. 6 sheets totalling 1,459 rows in the Fig 2A titration file; 663 rows in Fig 3A). Grepped the open-access full text for sample sizes and DNA sequences.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The DNA oligonucleotide sequences themselves are only in Supplementary Table S1, which I could not retrieve (Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out). The identity of the constructs (rDNA1, rDNA2, rDNA3, unimolecular G4, single-stranded DNA, double-stranded DNA, Myc double-stranded DNA) comes from the text and file names, not from any column in the data. The four 18 MB TIFF gel images were not downloaded (metadata only).

a1_downloadable.note: Zenodo record 20936879 is open, CC-BY-4.0, no login; I downloaded six files successfully.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No prediction target is a column. A per-sequence label (does this DNA promote CSB droplet formation, and how strongly does it partition in) would have to be constructed by aggregating hundreds of per-droplet rows across replicate blocks stacked horizontally inside each sheet, then dividing droplet by background intensity. Verified in the files.

a3_inputs_present.note: The DNA sequences, the only plausible model input, are absent from every file I opened; sheets and file names carry nicknames only (rDNA1, uG4, ssDNA, dsDNA). Sequences sit in Supplementary Table S1, which I could not retrieve.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are inconsistent within one column: in Fig 3A the same 'Area' header holds background values near 13,000-20,000 (pixels squared) and droplet values near 0.5-5 (micrometres squared). Fluorescence 'Mean' is in arbitrary camera units. Only 'Volume (uM^3)' is labelled.

a5_enough_rows.note: Thousands of per-droplet rows exist (1,459 rows across the 6 sheets of one titration file), but the independent unit is the DNA construct and condition: about 7 distinct DNA constructs, a handful of salt and oligo concentrations, 2-3 replicates. Far under the 1,500-row (or 400 for classification) bar for any sequence-to-phase-separation model.

a6_fits_laptop.note: All 27 files total 82.6 MB; the 23 tabular files total about 9 MB. Verified from the Zenodo file listing.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Nothing to contradict: the full text states no droplet counts or 'n =' values that I could grep, so paper and files cannot be cross-checked. Unverifiable rather than inconsistent.

a8_label_provenance.note: Measurements are real microscopy-derived quantities, not another model's output. But derived columns leak by construction: 'Radius' and 'Volume (uM^3)' are arithmetic functions of 'Area', so any model predicting one from the other is trivial.

existing_models.name: LLPSense (machine-learning framework for condition-dependent protein phase separation, 2025/2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond search-result abstract; reported as accurate condition-aware prediction of phase separation from protein language model embeddings plus environmental parameters.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Abstract states that existing models infer phase separation from amino-acid sequence alone and miss context-dependent behaviour.

existing_models.name: amyloid-predict and LLPS-predict (protein language model classifiers of phase-transition propensity, PNAS)
existing_models.score_and_split: Described in the abstract as open-source proteome-scale classifiers; no number verified by me.

existing_models.name: DeepG4 / G4-Attention / TransG4 (deep-learning predictors of DNA G-quadruplex formation)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported state-of-the-art accuracy on G4-sequencing-derived benchmarks; numbers not verified by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Interpretability and long-range base dependencies, per the TransG4 abstract.

backbone.name: None applicable at this scale (ESM-2 for CSB protein or DNABERT-2 for the oligos would have about 7 input items)
backbone.hardware: CPU only; irrelevant given sample size

integration.partner_dataset: None usable: the files carry no standard identifier (no UniProt accession, no genomic coordinates, no sequence).
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written: with construct nicknames only and no sequences or coordinates in the data, there is nothing to join on.

controls.positive_control: Would exist in principle (droplet area must predict droplet volume), but it is pure arithmetic, not biology.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is runnable on the droplet tables, but there is no meaningful label to shuffle.
controls.external_validation: None: no second dataset measures CSB droplet partitioning of these constructs.

honest_claim_h3: At most: 'among 7 DNA constructs assayed in one lab, multimolecular G-quadruplex-containing DNA raises CSB droplet count and lowers in-droplet mobility' — which is the paper's own conclusion from its own statistics, not a model's claim.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a DNA sequence to predict whether it drives a repair protein to form liquid droplets.
plain_idea.train_on: The idea considered was: one row per DNA oligonucleotide plus buffer condition, with the sequence as input. The deposit covers only about 7 distinct DNA constructs, so there are roughly a few dozen condition-level examples, not thousands.
plain_idea.predict: Whether, and how strongly, the DNA partitions into Cockayne syndrome B protein droplets. The true answer comes from confocal microscopy: droplet counts and the ratio of fluorescence inside droplets to background, measured by hand-drawn regions in image-analysis software.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups studying how DNA structure organises nuclear condensates would care, but this deposit is figure source data for one protein and a handful of oligos, so nothing could be learned about new sequences.

more_or_better_data.why: About 7 DNA constructs and one purified protein, against G-quadruplex predictors trained on genome-wide G4-sequencing data and phase-separation predictors trained on thousands of proteins.

confidence_score.why: Replicates exist (2-3 per condition), so noise is estimable, but with 7 constructs there is no population over which to calibrate per-prediction confidence.

models_beatable.why: The relevant open models (TransG4, G4-Attention, LLPS-predict) are 2024-2026 and use protein or DNA language-model backbones; this data cannot train anything comparable.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on every condition: no shared split, no shared measurement, and no join key in the files to attach any outside data to.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict from DNA sequence whether it promotes Cockayne syndrome B liquid-liquid phase separation and partitions into the resulting droplets, using the Zenodo droplet-count, droplet-size and FRAP tables as labels. Dead because the deposit contains about 7 DNA constructs and no sequences.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, nothing timed beyond parsing 6 files in seconds: the 23 tabular files total about 9 MB, so compute is trivial; the 20 hours is unpicking repeated 'REP n' header blocks spread across up to 66 columns in 21 workbooks and recovering sequences from a supplementary table.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the distinct DNA constructs in the file names and sheet names: rDNA1, rDNA2, rDNA3, ssDNA, dsDNA, uG4, Myc-dsDNA — about 7. That one count kills it in two minutes.

verdict_reason: Figure source data from a single-protein biophysics study: four Part A killers fail. A5, about 7 distinct DNA constructs and a few dozen condition-level units despite thousands of per-droplet rows; A3, the DNA sequences are not in any file; A2, a per-sequence label would have to be built by aggregating replicate blocks; A4, the same 'Area' header mixes pixels squared and micrometres squared within one sheet. Verified by opening six of the 27 files. The two plausible tasks it gestures at (sequence-to-G4-formation, sequence-to-phase-separation) already have open 2024-2026 models trained on orders of magnitude more data.
